For many Protestants, the Bible did not come from history. It descended from heaven, already shrink-wrapped, with Paul’s missionary maps included.

This is not their fault. It is a symptom.

The symptom has a name. Call it canon imperialism. Call it the assumption that the sixty-six-book Protestant Bible, assembled in the sixteenth century by reformers working under political pressure, is the natural shape of Scripture. Handed down. Settled. Done. The way the sky is blue and the grass is green. The Western church did not announce this assumption. It didn’t have to. Assumptions that large never announce themselves. They simply become the air you breathe.

So let us open a window.

The Bible you grew up holding was not the Bible of the early church. It was not the Bible of the church fathers. It was not the Bible of the councils that defined the Trinity and settled Christology. Athanasius, the man who gave you the Nicene faith, worked from a longer text world than your study Bible acknowledges. He quoted books your pastor has never preached from. He did not consider them secondary. He considered them the same air.

The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church carries eighty-one books in its canon. Eighty-one. It has carried them since the fourth century. The Ge’ez translations of those texts, including 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Meqabyan, were not produced by mystics operating outside the church. They were produced by the church. The Nine Saints. The Aksumite mission. The same tradition that received the faith before Constantine made Christianity a Roman political project.

The West inherited a canon shaped by Jerome, refined under political negotiation, then dramatically narrowed by Luther, who wanted to remove Hebrews, James, Jude, and Revelation from his own shortened version. He called James “an epistle of straw.” He kept it because the reformers around him pushed back. The canon you call settled was one man’s bad mood away from being even smaller.

And the translations, the Old Testament your Bible contains is largely translated from the Masoretic Text, a Hebrew tradition standardized by Jewish scribes between the seventh and tenth centuries A.D. The Septuagint, the Greek translation used by the apostles, used by Jesus Himself when he quoted Scripture, differs from the Masoretic in hundreds of places. Not in flavor. In content. In numbers. In names. In prophetic weight. Luke quotes Isaiah from the Septuagint. Paul builds his theology on Septuagint readings. The earliest Christians did not have a Hebrew Old Testament. They had a Greek one. The church ran on that Greek one for three centuries before Jerome went back to Hebrew.

And Jerome made choices. Every translator makes choices. Every choice is a theology.

None of this means your Bible is useless. It means it is located. It has a tradition, a history, a set of hands it passed through. Some of those hands were faithful. Some were political. Some were brilliant. Some were afraid. Every one of them was human.

The Ethiopian canon was also shaped by human hands. This is not an argument for perfect tradition. It is an argument against the pretense of no tradition. The Protestant who believes he reads “just the Bible” reads a canon assembled by reformers, printed by European presses, distributed by colonial missionaries, and received as the default. That is not nothing. That is a very specific something. Naming it honestly is not an attack on Scripture. It is respect for it.

The horizon is wider than you were shown.

The books you were told to ignore were not ignored by the early church. The texts you were taught to call “apocryphal” — the word means hidden, not false — were hidden from you, not from the tradition. Jerome hid them. Luther moved them to the back. Committees in the nineteenth century finished the work and removed them entirely from the common Bible. That removal is recent. It is not ancient. It is not settled.

You did not receive the oldest tradition.

You received the youngest major canon in Christianity. You received it as if it were the first.

There is no shame in that. Shame is for the man who knows and will not move. The reader who has come this far has already moved. The stone has been turned over. The name underneath is older than you thought.

The question now is what you do with that.

KingdomCode publishes from the Ethiopian Orthodox 81-book canon. If this is the first stone you’ve turned, there are eighty more.
